$comment: Pinned known-answer vectors for ChaCha20, transcribed BY HAND from RFC 8439.
They live in JSON rather than in TypeScript so that scripts/check-vectors.mjs
reads the SAME BYTES the lab does, with no transpiler and no regex over source
between them. An earlier draft parsed these out of the .ts file; a parser that
quietly matches fewer cases than exist is how a check becomes decoration.
Every value here is re-derived on every CI run by scripts/check-vectors.mjs
using Node's OpenSSL ChaCha20 -- an implementation sharing not one line with
this repository. That is what caught the one byte-range this transcription got
wrong: the tail of Appendix A.1 vector 4, from offset 44 onward.
mustDiffer is THIS LAB'S OWN addition and is labelled as such on the page,

source.name: RFC 8439
source.detail: the ChaCha20 and Poly1305 specification — §2.3.2, §2.4.2 and Appendix A.1

guard.why: the §2.3.2 case, named separately so check-vectors.mjs can pin OpenSSL's 16-byte IV packing before it judges any other case as a transcription error

blockCases.label: RFC 8439 §2.3.2
blockCases.why: the worked example the specification uses to show the block function, with a non-zero nonce and a counter of 1

blockCases.label: RFC 8439 A.1 #1
blockCases.why: an all-zero key and nonce at counter 0 — the degenerate input, which a build that mishandles the constants gets wrong

blockCases.label: RFC 8439 A.1 #2
blockCases.why: the same all-zero key and nonce one block later — it differs from the case above ONLY in the counter, so a build that ignores the counter fails here

blockCases.label: RFC 8439 A.1 #3
blockCases.why: one bit set in the last byte of the key — the smallest possible change to the key, and the answer is unrecognisable

blockCases.label: RFC 8439 A.1 #4
blockCases.why: the vector whose hand transcription was wrong from offset 44 when this file was first written, and which the independent check caught

blockCases.label: RFC 8439 A.1 #5
blockCases.why: an all-zero key with one bit set in the NONCE — so a build that ignores the nonce passes every vector above and fails this one

streamCases.label: RFC 8439 §2.4.2
streamCases.why: the specification’s encryption example — 114 bytes of real text, so the keystream is exercised across a block boundary rather than only at offset 0
streamCases.plaintext: Ladies and Gentlemen of the class of '99: If I could offer you only one tip for the future, sunscreen would be it.

mustDiffer.label: counter changed
mustDiffer.why: the published case at counter 2 instead of 1 — an implementation that ignored the counter would reproduce the counter-1 answer here

mustDiffer.label: one key bit changed
mustDiffer.why: the published case with the lowest bit of the key flipped — an implementation that ignored part of the key would reproduce the published answer

mustDiffer.label: one nonce bit changed
mustDiffer.why: the published case with one nonce bit flipped — this is the input a build is most likely to drop, because five of the six published vectors have an all-zero nonce
